sources.title: Wikipedia GeoSearch sweep, downtown Detroit (42.3314, -83.0458, 2.5 km radius, 200 results)

stops.name: Philip A. Hart Plaza
stops.description: This 14-acre riverfront plaza sits on the ground where Cadillac planted Fort Pontchartrain in 1701, and its centerpiece is Isamu Noguchi's stainless steel Dodge Fountain.

stops.name: Monument to Joe Louis
stops.description: A 24-foot bronze arm ending in a clenched fist hangs from a pyramid frame at Jefferson and Woodward, honoring the Detroit heavyweight who fought Jim Crow as well as opponents.

stops.name: The Spirit of Detroit
stops.description: Marshall Fredericks' 26-foot seated bronze has guarded the city hall steps since 1958, and Detroiters dress it in an oversized jersey whenever a local team makes a playoff run.

stops.name: Guardian Building
stops.description: Detroiters call this 1929 National Historic Landmark the Cathedral of Finance, and its orange brick tower and tiled lobby are open to anyone who walks in off Griswold.

stops.name: Penobscot Building
stops.description: Detroit's tallest building for nearly fifty years after 1928, it is still the one you find at night by the red beacon burning at the top of its spire.

stops.name: David Stott Building
stops.description: The last big skyscraper Detroit finished before the Depression stopped construction cold, this 1929 Art Deco shaft narrows as it rises and carries sculpture by Corrado Parducci.

stops.name: Book Tower
stops.description: Louis Kamper's 1926 Italian Renaissance tower stood empty for decades before a restoration reopened it to the public in 2023.

stops.name: Michigan Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument
stops.description: Unveiled in 1872 at the point where five of Detroit's main streets meet, this Civil War monument is crowned by an Amazon figure representing the state itself.

stops.name: Bagley Memorial Fountain
stops.description: The only surviving Henry Hobson Richardson work in the Detroit area, this 1887 granite drinking fountain spent seven years in storage before being reassembled in Cadillac Square.

stops.name: Wayne County Building
stops.description: Two bronze quadrigas named Victory and Progress ride the roofline of this 1902 Roman Baroque courthouse, one of the most heavily sculpted buildings in the city.

stops.name: Second Baptist Church
stops.description: Founded in 1836 by thirteen former slaves, the oldest Black congregation in the Midwest sheltered roughly 5,000 people in a room beneath its sanctuary on their way to Canada.

stops.name: Saints Peter and Paul Jesuit Church
stops.description: Built of Detroit common brick in 1848, this is the oldest church building still standing in the city and it still says Sunday mass.

stops.name: Mariners' Church
stops.description: Crews moving this 1849 stone church 880 feet east in 1955 found an Underground Railroad tunnel beneath it, and its bell rang 29 times for the crew of the Edmund Fitzgerald.

stops.name: Detroit Opera House
stops.description: Opened in 1922 as a movie palace said to be the fifth largest in the world, it was rescued from demolition and reopened in 1996 with Pavarotti singing.

stops.name: Fox Theatre
stops.description: The largest surviving movie palace of the 1920s seats over 5,000 people under a ceiling of mixed Burmese, Persian and Chinese ornament, and it still books live shows.

note: Detroit has never come up in this file's history, so it wins the rotation outright over every other never-run city on alphabetical tiebreak (next up: Green Bay, Houston, Indianapolis). Swept with the Wikipedia GeoSearch API over a 2.5 km radius on downtown Detroit, which returned 200 geotagged articles, then opened 20 individual articles to verify. All 15 stops here were verified article by article for current existence, location and public visibility; none are demolished or closed. Twelve have a verified street address and ZIP. Three are monuments in public squares with no street number of their own (Joe Louis fist at the Jefferson/Woodward median, Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument at the southeast tip of Campus Martius, Bagley Fountain in Cadillac Square) and are left address-null and zip-null rather than given a made-up number; each is easy to place from its article coordinates. WARNING ON ZIP SOURCING: Nominatim returned two wrong postcodes that were caught by cross-check, so do not trust it blind for downtown Detroit. It gave the Guardian Building 48224 (a far east side ZIP; correct is 48226) and the Fox Theatre 48226 (correct is 48201, which the Wikipedia infobox and the venue both give). It also mislabels downtown neighborhoods, filing Greektown addresses under Midtown. All ZIPs above were confirmed against a second source. Verified but held back to keep the batch a walkable Woodward-spine loop of about one mile from Hart Plaza up to the Fox: Comerica Park (2100 Woodward Ave, 48201) and Ford Field (2000 Brush St, 48226), both real and both on the spine but modern stadiums rather than historic core; Westin Book Cadillac Hotel (1114 Washington Blvd, 48226), dropped only as redundant with the neighboring Book Tower; Fort Street Presbyterian Church (631 W Fort St, 48226), a strong stop that was the tallest building in the state from 1877 to 1909 but sits west off the spine and would have made a fourth church; and John K. King Books (901 W Lafayette Blvd, 48226), an iconic million-volume store in a former glove factory but roughly 0.7 miles southwest of the core. Any of those five is ready to add if a longer or differently shaped route is wanted. Dropped outright during the sweep: People Mover stations, demolished buildings such as the J. L. Hudson store and Madison-Lenox Hotel, Joe Louis Arena (demolished), and articles about events, riots and companies rather than places.
